title: Simple harmonic motion, wave propagation and sound
summary: Recognize restoring forces, oscillation periods, wave speed and basic sound behavior.
concept: Simple harmonic motion has acceleration proportional and opposite to displacement from equilibrium. Mechanical traveling waves transport energy; their speed relates frequency and wavelength. Sound is a mechanical pressure wave and requires a medium.

formulas.note: Ideal mass–spring oscillator with negligible damping; T is in seconds.
Wave speed in medium v, frequency f, wavelength λ; intensity is power per area.

method: Distinguish oscillation frequency from wave speed, identify equilibrium and medium conditions.
guardrail: A wave's frequency generally stays fixed when entering a new medium, while its wavelength changes; sound does not propagate through vacuum.

worked.title: Mass–spring period
worked.problem: A mass of 0.50 kg is attached to an ideal spring of stiffness 200 N/m. Find the period.
worked.check: Frequency is inverse of period; oscillation is faster for a stiffer spring.
worked.takeaway: The period does not depend on amplitude for an ideal linear spring.

checks: If frequency doubles in the same medium, what happens to wavelength?
It halves.
At constant speed, λ=v/f.
Where is acceleration largest in an ideal mass–spring oscillator?
At maximum displacement.
a=−ω²x, so its magnitude grows with |x|.

title: Hydrostatic pressure, Pascal's principle and buoyancy
summary: Analyze pressure variation with depth and upward buoyant forces in fluids.
concept: Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth in a stationary fluid. A pressure change in an enclosed fluid is transmitted throughout the fluid. Archimedes' principle states that buoyancy equals the weight of displaced fluid, not necessarily the object's weight.

formulas.note: Uniform-density stationary liquid, depth h measured below reference surface.
Buoyant force is upward; displaced volume is the submerged fluid volume.

method: Define gauge versus absolute pressure and calculate displaced volume instead of assuming an object is fully submerged.
guardrail: Floating bodies displace their own weight of fluid; a submerged body displaces volume equal to its submerged volume.

worked.title: Buoyancy of an immersed cube
worked.problem: A cube of side 0.10 m is fully immersed in fresh water (ρ=1000 kg/m³). Find buoyant force using g=9.8 m/s².
worked.strategy: Calculate displaced volume and use Archimedes' principle.
steps: Force acts vertically upward through the center of buoyancy.
worked.check: The result equals the weight of 1 kg of displaced water.
worked.takeaway: Distinguish buoyant force from net upward force after subtracting the object's weight.

checks: Does hydrostatic gauge pressure depend on container shape at a given depth?
No, for a stationary uniform-density liquid.
p−p0=ρgh depends on depth, density and g.
Can a fully submerged steel object have an upward buoyant force while sinking?
Yes.
Gravity can exceed buoyancy even though buoyancy acts upward.

title: Continuity, Bernoulli's equation and fluid flow
summary: Use continuity and Bernoulli's relation under clearly defined flow assumptions.
concept: Mass conservation in steady flow implies a constant mass-flow rate through a streamtube. For an incompressible fluid, smaller flow area means larger speed. Bernoulli's equation represents mechanical-energy conservation along a streamline for steady, inviscid, incompressible flow without shaft work.

formulas.note: Second form assumes the same constant density at both sections.
Along a streamline under ideal Bernoulli assumptions.

method: Check the flow assumptions and continuity first, then compare pressure, kinetic and elevation terms.
guardrail: Do not apply ideal Bernoulli blindly across pumps, major viscous losses or rapidly unsteady flow; real systems may require head-loss terms.

worked.title: Flow through a narrow pipe
worked.problem: Water moves at 2 m/s in a pipe of area 6 cm². It enters a throat of area 2 cm². Find the throat speed for steady incompressible flow.
steps: The throat velocity is three times the initial velocity.
worked.check: Both areas use the same unit, so their ratio is dimensionless.
worked.takeaway: A smaller area increases speed at fixed incompressible flow rate.

checks: For a level ideal streamtube, what usually happens to static pressure where speed rises?
Static pressure decreases.
At fixed elevation, p+½ρv² remains constant under Bernoulli assumptions.
What is the SI unit of volumetric flow rate Q=Av?
m³/s.
Area m² times speed m/s.

title: Temperature, heat transfer, thermal expansion and calorimetry
summary: Distinguish temperature from heat and analyze energy transfer and thermal response.
concept: Temperature measures thermal state, while heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Heat may be conducted, convected or radiated. Calorimetry balances energy gained and lost within an insulated system; expansion coefficients approximate small temperature changes.

formulas.note: No phase change; c and α taken constant over the temperature interval.

formulas.latex: \dot Q_{\rm cond}=kA\frac{\Delta T}{L},\quad P_{\rm rad}=\varepsilon\sigma A(T^4-T_{\rm env}^4)
formulas.note: Steady planar conduction; net radiation assumes a suitable emissivity approximation and Kelvin temperatures.

method: Convert to Kelvin for temperature powers, distinguish heat capacity from specific heat and account for energy conservation.
guardrail: Heat has units joules, not degrees Celsius. Use Kelvin for blackbody T⁴ radiation and absolute thermodynamic formulas.

worked.title: Heat a water sample
worked.problem: How much energy heats 0.50 kg of water from 20°C to 40°C? Take c=4180 J/(kg·K), neglect losses.
worked.check: ΔT in K and °C has equal numerical size for a temperature difference.
worked.takeaway: Temperature change is not the same as final absolute temperature.

checks: Which heat transfer mode can operate through vacuum?
Thermal radiation.
Conduction and convection require material media.
A 1 m bar expands by 1 mm on heating. What is the strain?

title: Electric charge, Coulomb's law and electric fields
summary: Apply charge conservation, Coulomb force direction and electric field definitions.
concept: Electric charge is conserved and quantized. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. The electric field at a point is the force per unit positive test charge, and fields from multiple sources combine by vector superposition.

formulas.note: Point-charge electrostatics; use signed direction separately.
For a point charge in vacuum at distance r.

method: Locate source and test charges, draw force/field directions, then sum vector contributions.
guardrail: The electric field of a positive source points away; a negative source points toward it. An electron's force is opposite the field.

worked.title: Electric force between point charges
worked.problem: Charges +2 μC and −3 μC are 0.30 m apart in vacuum. Find force magnitude with k≈8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C².
worked.strategy: Use Coulomb's law and determine attraction or repulsion from the signs.
steps: Unlike charges attract along their line of separation.
worked.check: Coulomb-law inverse-square dependence: doubling r would quarter the force.
worked.takeaway: Magnitude calculations use absolute charge; direction comes from signs and geometry.

checks: What is electric field direction due to an isolated negative point charge?
Radially inward.
A positive test charge would be attracted.
If separation doubles, what happens to the Coulomb force magnitude?
It becomes one-quarter.
Inverse-square law, with all else fixed.
reference: Young & Freedman 13th; Serway & Jewett 9th; Cutnell & Johnson 9th

title: Electric potential, current, resistance and DC circuits
summary: Relate voltage to energy, current to charge flow and resistance to circuit behavior.
concept: Electric potential difference is energy change per unit charge. Electric current is charge transferred per time. Ohm's law for ohmic conductors relates voltage, current and resistance; Kirchhoff's laws express charge and energy conservation in lumped circuits.

formulas.note: Ohm's law is for an ohmic element under applicable conditions.
Resistor power is dissipative for passive sign convention.

method: Choose voltage polarities and current arrows; calculate series/parallel equivalent resistances or use Kirchhoff equations.
guardrail: A component's polarity depends on the assumed current direction and circuit arrangement. Electric potential (V) is not potential energy (J).

worked.title: Series resistors
worked.problem: Two ideal resistors 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series across a 20 V DC source. Find current and total power.
worked.strategy: Sum series resistance and apply Ohm's law.
worked.check: Individual drops are 8 V and 12 V, totaling 20 V.
worked.takeaway: In series, the same current passes through each resistor.

checks: What is the SI unit of electric current?
Ampere (A), equal to coulomb per second.
I=dQ/dt.
What happens to equivalent resistance when adding another positive resistor in parallel?
It decreases.
Parallel conductance increases.
reference: Young & Freedman 13th; Serway & Jewett 9th; Schaum's College Physics 9th

title: Magnetic fields, magnetic forces and magnetic materials
summary: Recognize magnetic force direction and basic fields from currents and materials.
concept: A magnetic field exerts force on a moving charge proportional to its velocity component perpendicular to the field. A current-carrying wire also experiences force in a field. Magnetic dipoles and magnetic properties of matter are useful for understanding motors and inductive devices.

formulas.note: Magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity and field; q is signed.
Uniform straight segment in uniform B; second formula for a long straight wire.

method: Use a right-hand rule for positive charge/conventional current, reverse the force direction for negative charge.
guardrail: The magnetic force on a moving point charge does no work because it is perpendicular to instantaneous velocity; a magnetic field alone cannot change speed.

worked.title: Wire in a magnetic field
worked.problem: A 0.20 m wire carries 5 A perpendicular to a uniform 0.30 T field. Find force magnitude.
steps: Force direction is perpendicular to both the wire current and field.
worked.check: Zero force if the same current direction becomes parallel to B.
worked.takeaway: Use the actual current direction to determine vector force.

checks: Does a stationary charge experience a magnetic Lorentz force?
No.
qv×B=0 when v=0.
What is the SI unit of magnetic flux density B?
Tesla (T).
One tesla is N/(A·m).

title: Faraday's law and introductory electromagnetic induction
summary: Explain induced EMF from changing magnetic flux and use Lenz's law for direction.
concept: Magnetic flux through a surface depends on field strength, area and orientation. A change in flux induces an EMF around a circuit. The induced current direction opposes the change in flux that produces it, consistent with energy conservation.

formulas.note: The N-turn form assumes equal flux per turn and consistent winding orientation.
Average EMF magnitude; flux in webers and time in seconds.

method: Define the area normal, determine whether flux increases or decreases and then assign induced EMF sign using Lenz's law.
guardrail: A magnetic field need not be changing everywhere; a changing circuit orientation or area can also change magnetic flux.

worked.title: Induced EMF in a coil
worked.problem: A 100-turn coil experiences a decrease in flux per turn from 0.020 Wb to 0.005 Wb in 0.50 s. Find average induced EMF magnitude.
steps: Magnitude of flux change per turn=|0.005−0.020|=0.015 Wb.
worked.check: Wb/s is volt; sign depends on chosen loop orientation.
worked.takeaway: Flux is a signed surface integral, not simply field strength.

checks: If flux through a fixed loop stays constant, is there a net induced EMF from Faraday's law?
No.
dΦ/dt=0 under that idealized single-loop model.
What does the minus sign in Faraday's law signify?
Lenz's law direction.
The induced EMF opposes the flux change.

title: Reflection, refraction, mirrors and lenses
summary: Use ray directions, Snell's law and image equations in basic geometrical optics.
concept: Reflection makes incident and reflected angles equal about a surface normal. Refraction changes ray direction when light crosses media of different refractive indices. Thin-lens and spherical-mirror equations locate paraxial images under a consistent sign convention.

formulas.note: All angles measured from the normal; Snell's law assumes a planar interface between isotropic media.
Use a stated standard real-is-positive convention for thin lenses/mirrors.

method: Draw the normal and principal rays, label refractive indices and adopt one explicit sign convention.
guardrail: Angles are measured from the normal, not the interface. A virtual image and a real image may require different signs for di.

worked.title: Refraction from air to glass
worked.problem: A light ray travels from air (n1=1.00) into glass (n2=1.50), striking at 30° to the normal. Find refraction angle.
steps: The ray bends toward the normal in higher-index glass.
worked.check: θ2 < θ1, consistent with refraction into higher refractive index.
worked.takeaway: State angles with respect to the normal.

checks: At normal incidence, does a ray bend at a planar interface?
No.
The refracted direction remains along the normal, although speed changes.
What does a negative image distance mean under the real-is-positive thin-lens convention?
A virtual image.
The image lies on the incident-light side for the usual converging-lens diagram.
reference: Cutnell & Johnson 9th; Young & Freedman 13th; Serway & Jewett 9th
